question: Internal company emails released to the US House Judiciary Committee reveal that major platforms perceived participation in the Code of Practice on Disinformation and the Code of Conduct on Hate Speech as ‘effectively mandatory’, with agendas ‘set under strong impetus from the EU Commission’ and ‘consensus’ achieved under heavy regulatory pressure, especially once the Digital Services Act (DSA) was in sight. 1.

How does the Commission reconcile its public claim that these codes are purely voluntary self-regulatory instruments with the reality that companies understood nonparticipation as exposing them to heightened enforcement risks and future DSA sanctions of up to 6 % of their global turnover?

Does the Commission acknowledge that using the threat of future binding legislation and severe fines to steer ‘voluntary’ commitments can create a chilling effect on lawful political speech and incentivise platforms to over remove controversial but legal content, particularly on migration, COVID-19 and gender ideology?

Will the Commission publish all its guidance, instructions and meeting readouts related to these codes, so that citizens and Parliament can assess whether its conduct remained within the limits of content neutral regulation, or whether it effectively dictated substantive editorial lines for private platforms?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) Codes of conduct under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1 are voluntary instruments, as explicitly stated in Article 45 of the DSA. They are developed by stakeholders, for stakeholders, including platforms and civil society. Non-compliance with commitments in codes is not sanctionable as such.

However, if a signatory adheres to and complies with a code of conduct, this may be considered an appropriate risk mitigation measure2, supporting their compliance with the DSA. At the same time, the mere fact of participating in and implementing a code of conduct does not in itself presume compliance with the DSA.

The Commission assesses the compliance of providers of very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) with the DSA on a case-by-case basis as part of its potential investigations.

Both the Code of Conduct on Disinformation3 and the Code of Conduct on Countering Illegal Hate Speech Online4 were established on a voluntary basis by their signatories even before the adoption of the DSA (respectively in 2018 and 2016). At the signatories’ request, both have been updated and integrated into the DSA framework. The codes aim to uphold the freedom of expression while enhancing transparency.

The signatories of both codes are diverse, including providers of platforms of different sizes, civil society organisations, and other stakeholders56. The Commission respects transparency requirements by publishing key enforcement decisions on a dedicated website7. It also makes publicly available its meetings with interest representatives8.
Moreover, the DSA requires Commission and European Board for Digital Services conclusions related to the assessment, monitoring and evaluation of codes of conduct to be published.
